title: Work-From-Home Job Sent You a Check? Is It a Scam, and What Do I Do?
meta_description: The FTC says no honest employer sends a check and asks you to send part back. Don't send money, don't pay for a job, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
answer: Yes, it's a scam. The FTC says no honest employer will ever send you a check to deposit and then tell you to send part of the money on, or to buy gift cards with it. The check will bounce, and the bank will want you to repay the full amount. Don't send any money from the check. If you already did, contact the company you used to send it right away and ask to reverse the payment. Then report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

steps.name: Know the rule: real jobs don't work this way
steps.text: The FTC says no honest employer will ever send you a check to deposit and then tell you to send part of the money on, or to buy gift cards with it. If a new job asks you to do that, stop. It's a scam.

steps.name: Don't pay to get a job
steps.text: The FTC says honest employers, including the federal government, will never ask you to pay to get a job. Scammers ask you to pay for starter kits, so-called training, or certifications that turn out to be useless.

steps.name: Say no to reshipping
steps.text: Some fake jobs ask you to get packages at home, throw away the boxes and receipts, and mail the items on. The FTC says reshipping goods is never a real job. It's just being part of a scam.

steps.name: Don't trust a check that "cleared"
steps.text: The FTC says banks must make deposited money available quickly by law, but it can take weeks to find out a check is fake. Seeing the money in your account doesn't mean the check is good. Don't send any of it to anyone.

steps.name: Search the company before you say yes
steps.text: Search online for the company or the person hiring you, plus words like "scam," "review," or "complaint." The FTC says finding no complaints doesn't prove a company is honest, but finding some can warn you.

steps.name: Already sent money? Act now
steps.text: The FTC says to contact the company you used to send the money right away, like your bank, card company, payment app, wire service, or gift card company. Tell them it was a scam and ask them to reverse the payment, if they can.

steps.name: Report it
steps.text: Report the job scam to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. The FTC says you can also report it to your state attorney general. For fake checks, the FTC also lists the U.S. Postal Inspection Service.

details.heading: How the fake check job scam works
paragraphs: The FTC says scammers post job ads the same way honest employers do. You get hired fast, often for a work-from-home job. Then a check arrives, usually for more than you expected.

Next comes the ask. You're told to deposit the check and send part of the money to someone else, or to buy gift cards and send the numbers. The FTC lists fake jobs like mystery shopping and personal assistant work that use this trick.
The FTC says the check will bounce, and the bank will want you to repay the amount of the fake check. By then, the scammer has the money you sent, and you're stuck paying the bank back.

details.heading: Why a "cleared" check can still be fake
paragraphs: The FTC says that by law, banks have to make deposited money available quickly. So the money can show up in your account in a short time.
But the FTC also says it can take weeks for a bank to figure out that a check is fake. Even if you see the money in your account, that doesn't mean it's a good check.

The FTC's advice: never use money from a check to send gift cards, money orders, or cryptocurrency, or to wire money to anyone who asks you to. Don't rely on money from a check unless you know and trust the person who sent it.

details.heading: If you already sent money or shared personal details
paragraphs: Paid by credit or debit card: The FTC says to report it to your card company or bank right away and ask for your money back. Paid by wire transfer or a payment app: report it to that company right away and ask them to reverse the payment.

Paid with a gift card: The FTC says to contact the gift card company right away using the number on the back of the card, and to keep the card and receipt. Paid with cryptocurrency: contact the exchange or ATM operator right away. The FTC says crypto payments don't have the same legal protections as cards, so getting money back can be hard.
Gave personal details for "payroll"? The FTC says you may now have an identity theft problem. If you gave out your Social Security number, the FTC says to go to IdentityTheft.gov for steps.

faqs.q: Will a real employer ever send me a check and ask for some back?
faqs.a: No. The FTC says no honest potential employer will ever send you a check to deposit and then tell you to send part of the money on, or to buy gift cards with it. If a job asks you to do this, it's a scam.

faqs.q: The money showed up in my account. Doesn't that mean the check is real?
faqs.a: No. The FTC says banks must make deposited money available quickly by law, but it can take weeks to find out a check is fake. Seeing the money doesn't mean the check is good. When it bounces, the bank will want the money back from you.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay the bank back for a fake check?
faqs.a: The FTC says the bank will want you to repay the amount of the fake check. That's why the scam works: the scammer keeps the money you sent, and you're left owing the bank.

faqs.q: Is it normal to pay for training or a starter kit for a new job?
faqs.a: No. The FTC says honest employers, including the federal government, will never ask you to pay to get a job. Scammers ask you to pay for starter kits, so-called training, or certifications that turn out to be useless.

faqs.q: Where do I report a job scam?
faqs.a: Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. The FTC says you can also report it to your state attorney general. For a fake check, the FTC also lists the U.S. Postal Inspection Service.

warnings: Don't send money from a check you got from someone you don't know, even if your bank shows the money as available.
Never buy gift cards for a new employer. The FTC says no honest employer asks you to do that with check money.
A job that has you receive and mail out packages is not a real job. The FTC says reshipping is part of a scam.

target_questions: Is it a scam if a new job sends me a check and asks me to send money back?
Why did my bank say the check cleared if it was fake?
Do I have to pay the bank back for a fake check?
Should I pay for training or a starter kit for a work-from-home job?
How do I report a job scam?
uncertain: Neither fetched FTC page says exactly what to do with the bank after depositing a fake check (for example, calling the bank before acting). Some non-government sites advise that, but it is kept off the page.
The FTC fake check page says banks must make funds available quickly 'by law' but gives no number of days and names no law, so the page gives no time frame.
The FTC Job Scams page is dated March 2023; the fake check page is dated June 2025. Both were live on 2026-10-30.

The ReportFraud.ftc.gov home page returned only its title to an automated fetch on 2026-10-30, so the page says nothing about it beyond 'report it there,' which the FTC job and fake check pages both say.
The USPIS report page lists mail fraud but does not mention fake checks by name; it is cited because the FTC fake check page links to it.

The video's '$300' in the mock chat is fictional and is not on the page. The video's line 'it bounces, and the bank wants it all back from you' is the video's wording of the FTC's 'repay the amount of the fake check.'
The 'What To Do if You Were Scammed' page date was not captured in this fetch, so its source label has no date.
